questions.title: Parallel Streams — When They Help vs Hurt
questions.question: When do Java parallel streams improve performance, and when do they actually hurt it?
questions.direct_answer: **Parallel streams** use the **common ForkJoinPool** — help on large, CPU-bound, side-effect-free pipelines. Hurt on small data, IO-bound work, or when they **starve** other FJP users.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the conditions under which parallelism actually pays off, rather than assuming parallelStream() is always faster.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding parallelStream() to small collections or I/O operations, adding overhead with no benefit — or worse, blocking the shared ForkJoinPool with I/O and starving other tasks.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the NQ model (N = elements, Q = work per element), the SIZED and SUBSIZED spliterator characteristics required for efficient splitting, and how to use a custom ForkJoinPool to isolate parallel work from the common pool.

sections.title: Parallel Streams Use the Common ForkJoinPool — And Blocking Operations There Starve Your Entire Application
sections.content:
Calling `.parallel()` on a stream splits the workload across multiple threads using the **common ForkJoinPool**. This is the same pool used by CompletableFuture's default async methods. A slow parallel stream operation can **starve** all other concurrent work sharing this pool.

Parallel streams improve throughput only when three conditions are met: the data source **splits cheaply** (arrays and ArrayLists split in O(1); LinkedLists require O(n) traversal to find the midpoint), the per-element operation is **CPU-intensive** enough to justify the overhead (thread management, task splitting, result merging), and there are **enough elements** to amortize the fixed costs.

For small collections (under ~10,000 elements), the overhead of splitting and merging typically exceeds the parallelism benefit. For I/O-bound operations (HTTP calls, database queries), parallel streams are **actively harmful** — they block common pool threads, reducing available parallelism for the entire JVM.

The ordering guarantee is another hidden cost. `parallelStream().forEachOrdered()` forces sequential ordering of results, eliminating most parallelism benefit. Similarly, `limit()` and `findFirst()` on parallel streams perform poorly because they must coordinate across threads to maintain encounter order.

sections.title: When Parallel Streams Help and When They Hurt: The Decision Checklist
sections.content:
Before using `.parallel()`, check four conditions.

**1. Data source splits cheaply.** Arrays and ArrayLists split in O(1) — the array is divided by index. LinkedList requires O(n) traversal. HashSet and TreeSet split reasonably. Streams from `Files.lines()` or `BufferedReader` split poorly.

**2. Operation is CPU-bound.** Math-heavy transformations, encryption, compression, complex object construction benefit from parallelism. Simple field access, string concatenation, or list addition do not — the overhead exceeds the benefit.

**3. Collection is large enough.** Below ~10,000 elements, the fixed cost of thread management and result merging dominates. Profile to find the breakeven for your specific operation.

**4. No shared mutable state.** Parallel stream operations must be stateless and non-interfering. Accumulating into a shared ArrayList without synchronization causes data corruption — use `collect()` with thread-safe collectors instead.

```java
// Good: CPU-intensive on large array
long sum = LongStream.rangeClosed(1, 10_000_000)
    .parallel()
    .map(n -> expensiveComputation(n))
    .sum();

// Bad: I/O-bound — blocks common pool threads
list.parallelStream()
    .map(id -> httpClient.fetch(id))  // blocks pool threads
    .collect(toList());
```

To isolate parallel stream work from the common pool, submit the stream operation to a **custom ForkJoinPool**: `new ForkJoinPool(4).submit(() -> stream.parallel()...collect()).join()`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Splits work across the common ForkJoinPool** — the same pool shared with CompletableFuture; a slow stream starves other async work.
- **Three requirements: large dataset, CPU-intensive, splittable source** — 10,000+ elements; no I/O; ArrayList not LinkedList.
- **`sorted()` and `limit()` force sequential coordination** — negate most of the parallelism benefit.
- **I/O in parallel streams blocks pool threads** — use CompletableFuture with a dedicated executor instead.
- **For isolation: `new ForkJoinPool(4).submit(() -> stream.parallel()...)`**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Parallel streams split work across the common ForkJoinPool — the same pool shared with CompletableFuture, making them dangerous when used carelessly.

**Three conditions for parallel streams to help:**
- Data source splits cheaply: arrays and ArrayLists are O(1); LinkedList is O(n) — terrible for parallel splitting
- Operation must be CPU-intensive enough to justify overhead — roughly 10,000+ elements minimum
- No I/O — blocking pool threads without CPU benefit actively harms throughput

**Common pitfalls:**
- `forEachOrdered()` and `limit()` force sequential coordination — kills most of the parallelism benefit
- I/O-bound operations in parallel streams block pool threads — use CompletableFuture with a dedicated executor instead

**Isolation from common pool:**
- `new ForkJoinPool(4).submit(() -> stream.parallel()...collect()).join()`
- Prevents a slow parallel stream from starving all other async work in the JVM

I recommend parallel streams only for CPU-heavy computation on large arrays or ArrayLists. For I/O-bound work, CompletableFuture with explicit thread pools is safer and more controllable.

questions.title: Race Condition — How to Identify and Fix
questions.question: What is a race condition in Java, how do you identify one, and what are the standard ways to fix it?
questions.direct_answer: A race condition occurs when a program's correctness depends on the relative timing of thread executions, producing inconsistent results that vary non-deterministically between runs. They arise whenever multiple threads access shared mutable state and at least one access is a write, without proper synchronisation. Fixes include synchronisation, atomic variables, immutable data, or confining state to a single thread.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can recognise the check-then-act and read-modify-write patterns as race condition triggers.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Fixing only one access point (adding synchronized to the write but not the read, or vice versa), leaving the race condition partially intact.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that races are easiest to find with thread sanitizers or tools like Java PathFinder, Helgrind, or careful code review for non-atomic compound operations.

sections.title: Race Conditions Pass Every Test and Fail in Production — Because They Depend on Timing You Cannot Control
sections.content:
A **race condition** occurs when the correctness of a program depends on the relative timing of two or more threads — and the timing is not controlled by synchronization. The program produces different results depending on which thread reaches a critical section first.

The most insidious property of race conditions is that they are **non-deterministic**. They pass unit tests reliably because single-threaded test execution has consistent timing. They fail intermittently in production because CPU scheduling, GC pauses, and load variations change the thread interleaving.

The two most common patterns: **check-then-act** (check a condition, then act on it — another thread changes the condition between check and act) and **read-modify-write** (read a value, compute a new value, write it — another thread writes between your read and write).

Check-then-act: `if (map.containsKey(key)) { return map.get(key); }` — between `containsKey()` and `get()`, another thread can remove the key. The fix: use `map.getOrDefault(key, defaultValue)` or `computeIfAbsent()`.

Read-modify-write: `counter++` — read 5, compute 6, write 6. Two threads both read 5, both write 6 — one increment is lost. The fix: `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` or `synchronized`.

sections.title: Identifying Race Conditions: Code Review Patterns and Tool-Based Detection
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Race condition = correctness depends on uncontrolled thread timing** — passes tests, fails in production under load.
- **Check-then-act pattern** — `containsKey()` then `get()` races; fix with `computeIfAbsent()`.
- **Read-modify-write** — `counter++` is three non-atomic steps; fix with `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`.
- **`volatile` doesn't fix compound operations** — ensures visibility, not atomicity; `counter++` on volatile still races.
- **Detection: `jcstress` for aggressive scheduling tests; SpotBugs for static analysis**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A race condition means program correctness depends on thread timing that synchronization doesn't control — they pass tests and silently fail in production.

**Two main patterns:**
- Check-then-act: `containsKey()` then `get()` — another thread removes between the two calls; fix with `computeIfAbsent()`
- Read-modify-write: `counter++` reads, increments, writes in three non-atomic steps — two threads can interleave; fix with `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`

**volatile doesn't fix it:**
- `volatile` ensures visibility but not atomicity — `counter++` on a volatile int still loses updates under concurrent access

**Detection:**
- `jcstress`: tests with aggressive scheduling to surface races in controlled environments
- SpotBugs: static analysis for unsynchronized field access patterns
- Code review: flag any shared mutable state accessed without synchronization, atomic, or single-writer guarantee

I recommend treating shared mutable state as guilty until proven safe — every access needs synchronization, an atomic operation, or a volatile with a single-writer guarantee.

questions.title: Liveness Hazards: Deadlock, Livelock, and Starvation
questions.question: Explain deadlock, livelock, and starvation in Java concurrency. How do you detect and prevent each?

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to identify and reason about liveness failures — a sign of production concurrency experience.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Conflating deadlock (stuck forever) with livelock (threads keep running but make no progress). Both prevent progress but have very different root causes and detection strategies.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention lock ordering as the canonical deadlock prevention strategy, jstack/ThreadMXBean for runtime detection, and that tryLock() with timeout can break deadlocks at the cost of retry logic.

questions.direct_answer: Deadlock: threads wait forever in a cycle of lock dependencies. Livelock: threads keep changing state responding to each other but never progress. Starvation: a thread never gets CPU time or a lock because others always take priority. All three prevent useful work without necessarily crashing the JVM.

sections.title: Deadlock Is Two Threads Each Holding What the Other Needs — But Livelock and Starvation Are Harder to Diagnose
sections.content:
Two threads, each holding what the other needs — **deadlock** is the most recognizable liveness hazard, but not the only one. Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2. Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1. Neither can proceed. The JVM detects this in thread dumps — look for "waiting to lock" cycles.

**Livelock** is more subtle: threads are not blocked, they are actively executing — but they keep **changing state in response to each other** without making progress. Two people in a hallway stepping left and right simultaneously to avoid each other. The threads consume CPU but accomplish nothing, and no thread dump reveals the problem because no thread is BLOCKED or WAITING.

**Starvation** means a thread is perpetually denied the resource it needs. With unfair locks, a continuously arriving stream of threads can barge ahead of a waiting thread indefinitely. The starved thread is technically in a WAITING state but never progresses. Starvation is especially dangerous because the system appears to work — all other threads are making progress.

Deadlock requires four conditions simultaneously: **mutual exclusion** (resources are non-shareable), **hold and wait** (thread holds one resource while waiting for another), **no preemption** (resources cannot be forcibly taken), and **circular wait** (A waits for B, B waits for A). Breaking any one condition prevents deadlock.

sections.title: Prevention Strategies: Lock Ordering, Timeout, and Detection
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Deadlock** — circular wait; Thread A holds Lock 1, waits for Lock 2; Thread B vice versa; neither proceeds.
- **Fix: lock ordering** — all threads acquire locks in the same global order; circular wait condition can't form.
- **Livelock** — threads actively running but reacting to each other without progress; fix with randomized backoff.
- **Starvation** — thread perpetually denied resources by unfair lock; fix with fair mode (FIFO ordering).
- **`jstack` detects deadlock cycles automatically** — prints "Found N deadlock" section at the bottom of the dump.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Deadlock, livelock, and starvation are three distinct failure modes — they differ in what the threads are doing, how you diagnose them, and how you prevent them.

**Deadlock:**
- Two threads each holding what the other needs — Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2; Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1; neither proceeds
- Fix with lock ordering: all threads acquire locks in the same global order — circular wait condition can't form
- Diagnosis: `jstack` automatically detects monitor cycles and prints "Found N deadlock" at the bottom

**Livelock:**
- Threads are not blocked — they're actively running but keep reacting to each other without making progress
- Like two people stepping left and right in a hallway, each trying to let the other pass
- Fix with randomized backoff — break the symmetry

**Starvation:**
- A thread is perpetually denied resources — unfair locks let new arrivals barge ahead of waiting threads indefinitely
- Fix with fair locks or explicit priority management — trades throughput for guaranteed FIFO ordering

**Prevention tools:**
- `tryLock(timeout)` breaks hold-and-wait by releasing locks on timeout — essential for dynamic locking scenarios
- `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` for programmatic detection in health-check endpoints

I recommend lock ordering as the primary prevention strategy and `tryLock` with timeouts as the fallback.

questions.question: How do you detect a deadlock in a running Java application using a thread dump?
questions.title: Detecting Deadlock in Java — jstack, ThreadMXBean, and Dump Analysis
questions.direct_answer: Take a **thread dump** of the running JVM and look for threads in **`BLOCKED`** state waiting on monitors, plus the JVM's explicit **"Found one Java-level deadlock"** section at the bottom of the output. Three ways to capture: **(1) `jstack <pid>`** — the simplest, prints directly to stdout; **(2) `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`** — modern replacement, also works for virtual threads with `Thread.dump_to_file`; **(3) Send `SIGQUIT`** (`kill -3 <pid>` on Unix) — JVM prints dump to its stdout. Programmatically, use **`ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()`** — returns thread IDs of any deadlocked threads; this is how monitoring systems detect deadlocks automatically. For a textbook deadlock (thread A holds lock X, waiting for Y; thread B holds Y, waiting for X), the JVM auto-detects and reports the cycle. For livelocks or non-monitor-based deadlocks (e.g., on `ReentrantLock`), you must inspect the stack traces manually.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the mechanics of thread dumps, can read jstack/jcmd output, and knows about programmatic detection via ThreadMXBean
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only checking CPU usage (deadlocks are 0% CPU, not high). Not knowing jstack/jcmd syntax. Assuming all deadlocks are auto-reported — ReentrantLock deadlocks may require manual analysis
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention `jcmd Thread.print -l` for lock info; `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads` for automated alerting; that Java 21's thread dump format differs for virtual threads; and taking multiple dumps 5-10s apart to confirm the state is stable

sections.title: What a Deadlock Looks Like
sections.content:
A deadlock is a **cyclic wait**: two or more threads each holding a resource the other needs, neither can proceed. In Java, the classic case is two threads acquiring the same two monitor locks in opposite order:

```
Thread A: holds Lock1, waits for Lock2
Thread B: holds Lock2, waits for Lock1
```

Symptoms in production:
- Requests hang or time out.
- **CPU usage is near 0%** (threads are parked, not spinning).
- Heap doesn't grow (no OOM).
- Application appears frozen or extremely slow.
- Specific endpoints / features stop working; rest works.

The combination of **hung behavior + 0% CPU** is the strongest signal that it's a deadlock rather than a CPU-bound stall or a slow downstream. Next step: capture a thread dump.

sections.title: Capturing the Thread Dump
sections.content:
Three ways, in order of preference:

**1. `jstack <pid>`** — simplest, always works:
```bash
jps -l               # find the PID of your Java process
jstack 12345 > dump.txt
```
`-l` for lock info (recommended): `jstack -l 12345`. Shows which locks each thread holds.

**2. `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`** — modern replacement, works with virtual threads:
```bash
jcmd 12345 Thread.print -l
# Java 21 — dumps all threads including virtual to a file
jcmd 12345 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json
```

**3. `kill -3 <pid>`** (Unix) or **`Ctrl+Break`** (Windows console) — sends SIGQUIT; JVM prints dump to its stdout (where the app logs to). Useful when `jstack` can't attach (permissions) or you can't install JDK on the container.

**Rule: take at least two dumps 5–10 seconds apart**. If threads are at the same stack line in both dumps, they're genuinely stuck. If they've moved, it's not a deadlock — maybe just slow progress.

sections.title: Reading the Dump — The JVM's Auto-Detection
sections.content:
For deadlocks on **intrinsic monitor locks** (the `synchronized` keyword), the JVM runs its own deadlock detector when you take a dump. At the bottom of the output you'll see:

```
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"Thread-1":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f1c8c002e80 (object 0x00000000d5f6a7c8, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "Thread-0"
"Thread-0":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f1c8c004a38 (object 0x00000000d5f6a7d8, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "Thread-1"

Java stack information for the threads listed above:
===================================================
"Thread-1":
    at com.example.Deadlock.method2(Deadlock.java:35)
    - waiting to lock <0x00000000d5f6a7c8> (a java.lang.Object)
    - locked <0x00000000d5f6a7d8> (a java.lang.Object)
    at com.example.Deadlock.lambda$main$1(Deadlock.java:25)
"Thread-0":
    at com.example.Deadlock.method1(Deadlock.java:20)
    - waiting to lock <0x00000000d5f6a7d8> (a java.lang.Object)
    - locked <0x00000000d5f6a7c8> (a java.lang.Object)
```

The cycle is spelled out: each thread's **held lock** and **waited lock** plus the stack frames. This is typically all you need to find the bug — look at the line numbers and fix the lock ordering.

sections.title: ReentrantLock Deadlocks — No Auto-Detection
sections.content:
The JVM's built-in deadlock detector only finds **monitor (synchronized)** deadlocks. For `ReentrantLock`, `ReadWriteLock`, or `Semaphore` deadlocks, **there is no "Found deadlock" section** in the dump. You have to read manually.

In the dump, these threads appear in **`WAITING` (parking)** state with `LockSupport.park` on the stack:
```
"worker-2" #45 prio=5 os_prio=0 tid=0x... nid=0x... waiting on condition [0x00007f...]
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
        at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21/Native Method)
        - parking to wait for  <0x00000000d8b00af0> (a j.u.c.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync)
        at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(LockSupport.java:341)
        at j.u.c.locks.AbstractQueuedSynchronizer.acquire(AbstractQueuedSynchronizer.java:943)
        at j.u.c.locks.ReentrantLock$Sync.lock(ReentrantLock.java:156)
        at j.u.c.locks.ReentrantLock.lock(ReentrantLock.java:322)
        at com.example.Service.withdraw(Service.java:52)
```

To spot the cycle:
1. Find all threads parked on `ReentrantLock`.
2. For each, note which lock instance (`0x...` address) they're parked on.
3. Cross-reference which thread **holds** that lock (you need `ThreadMXBean` or `jcmd Thread.print -l` for full lock info).
4. If you find a cycle, that's your deadlock.

This is tedious. The better answer is **programmatic detection**.

sections.title: Programmatic Detection — ThreadMXBean
Interpreting Thread States in the Dump
sections.content:
Each thread's state in the dump tells you what to look for:

| State | What it means |
|---|---|
| **`RUNNABLE`** | Actually executing or ready to be scheduled. If stuck here, it's a live thread; check if it's in a tight loop. |
| **`BLOCKED`** | Waiting to acquire a **monitor** (`synchronized`). Look at `- waiting to lock <addr>` and find who holds it. |
| **`WAITING` (parking)** | Parked via `LockSupport.park` — typically `ReentrantLock` or other AQS-based wait. See `- parking to wait for <addr>`. |
| **`WAITING` (on object monitor)** | Called `Object.wait()` — waiting for a `notify`. Check who should be notifying. |
| **`TIMED_WAITING`** | Sleep, timed wait, or `Thread.sleep`. Not a deadlock source by itself. |
| **`NEW` / `TERMINATED`** | Not relevant. |

**For a deadlock investigation**:
1. Filter to `BLOCKED` and `WAITING (parking)` threads.
2. Look at their wait-on addresses.
3. Check who owns those addresses (top of stack `- locked <addr>`).
4. Cycle? That's your deadlock.

sections.title: Java 21 Virtual Thread Dumps
sections.content:
With virtual threads, a thread dump can include millions of entries. Two changes:

**1. Dedicated dump command**:
```bash
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json
# or text
jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=plain dump.txt
```
Compact, structured output including all virtual threads.

**2. JSON format** is easier to process programmatically — you can query for threads in specific states with `jq`:
```bash
jq '.threads[] | select(.state=="WAITING")' dump.json
```

**`jstack`** still works but only sees mounted virtual threads + platform threads. Use `Thread.dump_to_file` for a complete picture.

**`ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads`** still works for virtual threads. But `ThreadMXBean.dumpAllThreads` on a system with millions of virtual threads can be slow — reserve it for debugging, not hot paths.

sections.title: Production Practices
sections.content:
**Always in place**:
- **Automated deadlock detection** via scheduled `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` (every 30-60s).
- **Alert on detection** — page on-call; deadlocks rarely clear themselves.
- **Health checks that take a dump on hang** — periodic captures retained for forensic analysis.

**On incident**:
1. Take **two dumps** 5-10 seconds apart.
2. Compare: are threads at the same line in both? (yes → deadlock or stuck; no → slow progress).
3. Search for "Found one Java-level deadlock" — if present, you have your answer.
4. Otherwise: look at `BLOCKED` and `WAITING (parking)` threads, trace wait-on relationships.
5. Inspect code at the stack lines for lock-ordering violations.

**For reporting / escalation**:
- Capture dumps to logs when possible.
- Include timestamps.
- Annotate which threads form the cycle.

**Watch out for**:
- **Partial dumps**: if the JVM is unresponsive, `jstack` may hang. `jstack -F` (force) works but may not give clean output.
- **Container permissions**: in Kubernetes, your Java container may lack capabilities to ptrace itself. Use `-e JVM_ARG_ADD=-XX:+CreateCoredumpOnCrash` or plan `jcmd` paths.
- **Heap dumps ≠ thread dumps** — heap dumps are for memory issues; thread dumps for thread/deadlock issues. Don't confuse.
- **False positives**: threads that look stuck at the same stack for 10 seconds may just be waiting for slow I/O. Corroborate with metrics.

sections.content:
- **Symptoms of deadlock**: frozen app, near-0% CPU, hung requests.
- **Capture** with `jstack <pid>`, `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`, or `kill -3 <pid>` (SIGQUIT).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Deadlock detection has two flavors: manual thread dump analysis and programmatic via ThreadMXBean.

**Symptoms**
- Hung requests, frozen app
- CPU near 0% (threads parked, not spinning)
- Heap doesn't grow
- Specific endpoints stop responding

**Capturing a thread dump**
- `jstack <pid>` — simplest, prints to stdout
- `jstack -l <pid>` — includes lock info
- `jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l` — modern replacement
- `kill -3 <pid>` (SIGQUIT) — JVM prints dump to its stdout
- Take **two dumps 5-10s apart** to confirm threads are actually stuck

**Reading the dump**
- Look at bottom of output: **"Found one Java-level deadlock"** section
- JVM auto-detects monitor (`synchronized`) deadlocks and spells out the cycle
- Each thread shows: held monitor + waiting monitor + stack trace
- Line numbers tell you exactly where the bug is

**Thread states that matter**
- **`BLOCKED`** = waiting for monitor; see `- waiting to lock <addr>`
- **`WAITING (parking)`** = parked via `LockSupport.park`, typically `ReentrantLock`; see `- parking to wait for <addr>`
- **`WAITING (on object monitor)`** = `Object.wait()` — waiting for `notify`
- **`RUNNABLE`** threads stuck here = tight loop, not deadlock

**The ReentrantLock gap**
- JVM auto-detector **only covers `synchronized`**
- `ReentrantLock`, `ReadWriteLock`, `Semaphore` deadlocks do **NOT** appear in the "Found deadlock" section
- Must manually trace: threads parked → which lock instance → who holds it → is there a cycle?

**Programmatic detection — the production answer**
- `ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads()`
- Covers **all** lock types (monitor and Lock)
- Returns thread IDs; use `getThreadInfo(ids, true, true)` for full info
- Schedule every 30–60 seconds; alert on-call when it fires
- This is how real monitoring works at scale

**Java 21 virtual threads**
- Millions of threads makes a text dump huge
- Use `jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json` for structured output
- Query with `jq`
- `jstack` still works but only sees mounted + platform threads
- `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` still works

**Best practices**
- Always take **two dumps** 5-10s apart — confirms genuinely stuck
- In production, run `findDeadlockedThreads` periodically as part of health checks
- Alert immediately on detection — deadlocks rarely self-heal
- Annotate dumps with timestamp and which threads form the cycle before escalation

**Watch out for**
- **Container permissions**: ptrace/`jstack` may be blocked in Kubernetes; ensure `jcmd` paths work
- **Heap dumps ≠ thread dumps** — don't confuse the two
- **`jstack -F`** for force attach when JVM is unresponsive — last resort

**Recommendation:** Bake **automated deadlock detection** via `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` into every production service — run it on a 30–60 second schedule as part of health checks, and alert on-call the moment it fires. For on-demand debugging, use **`jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l`** (modern) or `jstack -l` (classic); always take **two dumps 5-10 seconds apart** to confirm threads are actually stuck versus making slow progress. Look for the **"Found one Java-level deadlock"** section for monitor deadlocks — the JVM hands you the cycle on a plate. For `ReentrantLock` deadlocks there's no auto-report, so know how to read the parked stack traces. On **Java 21**, use `jcmd Thread.dump_to_file -format=json` for dumps that include virtual threads. And don't confuse deadlock (0% CPU) with a tight loop (100% CPU) or slow downstream (some CPU, waiting on external) — each has a different fingerprint in a dump.

questions.question: How do you prevent deadlocks in Java? What design techniques avoid them?
questions.title: How to Avoid Deadlock in Java — Lock Ordering, tryLock, and Design Techniques
questions.direct_answer: Six proven techniques, roughly in order of effectiveness: **(1) Lock ordering** — always acquire locks in the same global order (e.g., by lock identity hash or by a documented precedence). Eliminates cyclic waits by construction. **(2) `tryLock(timeout)`** — use `ReentrantLock.tryLock(1, SECONDS)` instead of unconditional `lock()`; if it fails, release everything held and retry. **(3) Open calls** — never call external methods (callbacks, listeners, other services) while holding a lock; release first. **(4) Reduce lock scope** — minimize the code inside `synchronized` blocks; narrow the critical section. **(5) Lock-free alternatives** — `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicReference`, immutable data + atomic reference swap. **(6) Single global lock** — simple, no cycles possible; fine for low-contention scenarios. Bonus: **prefer `ReentrantLock` over `synchronized`** on Java 21 (no virtual-thread pinning, plus `tryLock` support). Actively monitor with `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()`. Most production deadlocks come from inconsistent lock ordering — enforce it via code review and static analysis.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning one technique. Assuming synchronized is always safe. Not recognizing that calling external methods while holding a lock is a common deadlock source
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give concrete ordering strategies (by identityHashCode, by documented precedence), mention the 'open calls' principle from Java Concurrency in Practice, cite tryLock patterns with backoff, and discuss lock-free alternatives as the ultimate avoidance

sections.title: The Four Coffman Conditions — Break Any One
sections.content:
Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions simultaneously:

1. **Mutual exclusion** — at least one resource is held exclusively. Usually unavoidable for correctness.
2. **Hold and wait** — a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
3. **No preemption** — a resource can't be forcibly taken from a thread.
4. **Circular wait** — threads form a cycle where each waits on the next.

Prevention means breaking at least one condition:
- **Lock ordering** breaks circular wait.
- **`tryLock` with timeout + back-off** breaks hold-and-wait (thread releases what it has on timeout).
- **Open calls** reduce hold-and-wait (don't hold locks across unknown code).
- **Lock-free data structures** eliminate mutual exclusion (break #1).

The most powerful in practice is **lock ordering** — it makes deadlock *impossible by construction*, and it costs nothing at runtime.

sections.title: The Classic Deadlock
Fix #1 — Lock Ordering by Identity Hash
Fix #2 — tryLock with Timeout and Back-off
Fix #3 — Open Calls (Don't Lock Across Unknown Code)
Fix #4 — Lock-Free Alternatives
Fix #5 — Reduce Lock Scope + Java 21 Considerations
Design Checklist
sections.content:
| Technique | When to Use | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| **Lock ordering** | Multiple locks, well-defined objects | Needs a global ordering rule enforced across codebase |
| **`tryLock` with timeout** | Can't easily enforce ordering; want graceful degradation | Risk of livelock without back-off |
| **Open calls** | Listener/callback patterns | Requires copying collections before iteration |
| **Reduce lock scope** | General best practice | Can require refactoring to separate concerns |
| **Lock-free alternatives** | Most shared state | Some patterns don't map cleanly (multi-field invariants) |
| **Single global lock** | Simple systems, low contention | Doesn't scale under high contention |
| **`ReentrantLock` over `synchronized`** | Java 21 virtual threads, needs `tryLock` | Must always `unlock` in `finally` |

**Watch out for**:
- **Reentrant deadlock-like freezes**: a thread re-acquiring a non-reentrant lock it already holds. Default `synchronized` and `ReentrantLock` are reentrant, so rare in practice.
- **Hidden locks in libraries**: third-party code may have internal `synchronized`. Audit hot paths.
- **Static initializer deadlocks**: class init holds a per-class lock; two classes each trying to init the other can deadlock.
- **ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent** holds a bucket lock during the lambda — never call out to other locks from inside.
- **Shutting down** executors while threads hold locks — can deadlock shutdown.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Lock ordering** is the most effective technique — consistent global order eliminates cyclic wait.
- **`tryLock` with timeout and back-off** gives graceful degradation; combine with ordering.
- **Open calls** — never call external code while holding a lock.
- **Reduce lock scope** — narrow critical sections, never include I/O or unknown methods.
- **Lock-free data structures** (`ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicReference`, immutable + atomic swap) eliminate the problem entirely.
- **Single global lock** is a fallback for simple, low-contention systems.
- **`ReentrantLock` > `synchronized`** on Java 21 (no pinning, has `tryLock`, `Condition`, fairness).
- **Monitor in production** with `ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` on a schedule; alert on-call.
- **Avoid holding locks across**: I/O, listeners, long CPU work, `Thread.sleep`, `wait`.
- **Static class initialization can deadlock** — keep it simple.
- **Document lock hierarchies** in architecture docs; enforce in code review.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions simultaneously — break any one and you're safe.

**1. Lock ordering — the cornerstone**
- Always acquire multiple locks in the same global order
- Order by **identity hash**: `System.identityHashCode(obj)` — smaller first
- Or by **domain ID**: `account.id` — lower ID first
- Or by **documented precedence**: "User before Order before Inventory"
- Zero runtime cost; deadlock impossible by construction
- Handle rare hash collisions with a tie-breaker lock

**2. tryLock with timeout and back-off**
- `ReentrantLock.tryLock(1, SECONDS)` — returns false if unavailable
- If can't get both locks, release what you have and retry
- No thread ever blocked while holding another lock
- Risk: livelock if two threads keep retrying in lockstep — add randomized `Thread.sleep` back-off
- `tryLock(timeout)` with a finite timeout lets you fail fast and return an error

**3. Open calls**
- **Never call external methods while holding a lock**
- Listeners, callbacks, other services — all unknown code
- They might acquire other locks or call back into you
- Pattern: copy collections under lock, iterate without:
  ```
  snapshot = copyOf(listeners);
  // release lock
  for (l : snapshot) l.onUpdate();
  ```
- Straight from Brian Goetz's *Java Concurrency in Practice*

**4. Reduce lock scope**
- Smaller critical sections = fewer opportunities for ordering bugs
- Never include I/O, heavy CPU, external calls, or `sleep` inside a lock
- Use pattern: compute outside, update inside

**5. Lock-free alternatives**
- `ConcurrentHashMap` with `computeIfAbsent` — atomic, lock-free for typical ops
- `AtomicReference` with `updateAndGet` — CAS-based
- Immutable data + `volatile` reference swap — readers never lock
- `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for read-heavy structures
- Ultimate avoidance: no locks, no deadlock possible

**6. Single global lock**
- One lock for the whole system
- No cycles possible (only one lock)
- Fine for simple, low-contention systems
- Doesn't scale but gives correctness

**Java 21 specific — prefer `ReentrantLock`**
- `synchronized` pins virtual threads to carriers
- Under load: carrier starvation
- `ReentrantLock` uses Loom-aware `LockSupport.park` — unmounts cleanly
- Also has `tryLock`, `Condition`, fairness options

**Monitoring in production**
- `ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads()` on a 30-60s schedule
- Alert on-call when it fires
- Capture thread dump automatically

**Common deadlock sources to audit**
- Transfers between two objects each with their own lock
- Nested services holding locks during callbacks
- ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent lambda that acquires another lock (bucket lock + extra lock = potential cycle)
- Static initializers with cross-class dependencies
- Shutdown sequences holding locks across pool termination

**Recommendation:** **Adopt lock ordering as the default** for any code that acquires multiple locks — order by identity hash or domain key, document the rule, enforce in code review. Layer in **`tryLock(timeout)`** for graceful degradation under extreme contention. **Apply the open-calls principle ruthlessly**: copy collections under lock, iterate without; never hold a lock across a listener callback or external call. For most shared state, **reach for lock-free alternatives first** — `ConcurrentHashMap`, `AtomicReference`, immutable-plus-swap; they sidestep the whole class of problems. On **Java 21+**, default to `ReentrantLock` over `synchronized`. And run **`ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads()` as a scheduled health check** so the first time a deadlock ever forms in production, you get paged instead of learning about it from customer complaints.
